title: The congregation
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: yesterday it was just you and a scale. today, the people around you. who do you feel most like yourself around?
options: there’s a word for that. listen.
then this one will feel close. listen.
that’s honest. this one is for you. listen.

steps.line: On his travels, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana came to a village where nobody would welcome them. People mocked them and shut their doors.
steps.label: a traditional sakhi

steps.line: As they left, the Guru turned and blessed the village: may you stay settled here, always.

steps.q: Mardana went everywhere with Guru Nanak. What did he carry?
o: A rabab, to play the hymns
A begging bowl for them both
steps.why: Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician, played the rabab while Guru Nanak sang. Wherever they went, the hymns came with them.

steps.line: At the next village, people ran out to meet them. They fed them, sang hymns with them, and gave them a place to sleep.

steps.q: Leaving this kind village, the Guru blesses it too. What do you think he says?
o: May you stay settled here, always
steps.why: Scattered. Now Mardana was really confused.

steps.line: As they left, he blessed them: may you be scattered. Mardana stopped in the road. Master, why bless the cruel to stay and the kind to scatter?
The Guru said: let the unkind stay where they are, so their ways don’t spread. Let the good scatter, and carry goodness wherever they go.

steps.q: You’re from the kind village, and your family scatters to new towns. By the Guru’s logic, what’s your job there?
o: Start a new circle of kindness
Keep your head down and fit in
steps.why: Good company is meant to travel. Every kind person who moves on can start a new circle.

steps.line: Sikhs call it sangat: the company you keep. The stories say that wherever Guru Nanak went, he left a small circle behind, to sing and share food.
steps.label: today

steps.q: The small circles Guru Nanak left behind met in places with a name of their own. What were they called?
steps.why: The early Sikh meeting places were dharamsals. Later they came to be called gurdwaras, the Guru’s door.

steps.q: In the langar, the free kitchen, everyone eats side by side on the floor. Why the floor?
o: Sitting low shows respect for food
So no one sits higher than anyone
steps.why: Sitting together in rows is called pangat. King or beggar, everyone sits at the same level and eats the same food.

say: here’s the heart of it. sikhs believe you become a little like the people you sit with. that’s why the gurus built sikh life around sangat: singing, eating and caring together.
there’s a long tradition that the guru is present wherever the sangat gathers. a person alone can drift. a person in good company gets carried, like a small boat on a current.

steps.q: From the story, what makes a sangat good, in the Guru’s eyes?
o: What it carries out into the world
How many people it can feed
steps.why: The kind village wasn’t blessed to stay. It was blessed to spread.

today.say: today, choose one circle that helps you remember what matters, and give it an hour this week. if you like, try a gurdwara’s evening kirtan, the hymn singing: just sit and listen. your choice.
options: then go be carried a little.
that’s okay. start with one friend who lifts you.

sources: Traditional sakhi of Guru Nanak blessing two villages (“vasde raho” for the unkind one, “ujjad jao” for the kind one), told widely in Sikh oral tradition and sakhi collections
Sikh teaching on sangat and sadh sangat, and the tradition that the Guru is present in the gathered sangat
check: The two-villages sakhi is a popular telling; I could not tie it to one Janamsakhi recension. Please confirm the source.
